{
  "file_path": "D:\\CelLab\\docs\\FILE_FORMATS.md",
  "content": "# CelLab input files: reference\n\nCelLab reads two kinds of JSON files:\n\n- an **automaton file** (`automata/*.json`) says *what the automaton is*: its states, neighbourhood, edges and rules;\n- an **experiment file** (`experiments/*.json`) says *what to do with it*: grid size, first generation, number of steps, seed, questions.\n\nCheck any file without running it:\n\n```bash\ncellab check automata/my_automaton.json experiments/my_experiment.json\n```\n\nEvery mistake is reported with the file, the field and the reason, for example\n`forest_fire.json, rules[1].when: 'self == FIER': unknown name 'FIER' (did you mean 'FIRE'?)`.\n\n---\n\n## Automaton file\n\n```json\n{\n  \"name\": \"Forest fire\",\n  \"description\": \"Optional free text.\",\n  \"dimensions\": 2,\n  \"states\": [\"EMPTY\", \"TREE\", \"FIRE\"],\n  \"neighbourhood\": \"von_neumann\",\n  \"edges\": {\"type\": \"fixed\", \"value\": \"EMPTY\"},\n  \"update\": \"synchronous\",\n  \"parameters\": {\"p\": 0.01},\n  \"rules\": [\n    {\"when\": \"self == FIRE\", \"then\": \"EMPTY\"},\n    {\"when\": \"self == TREE and count(FIRE) >= 1\", \"then\": \"FIRE\"}\n  ],\n  \"otherwise\": \"self\",\n  \"colors\": {\"EMPTY\": \"#e3dfd4\", \"TREE\": \"#4a7326\", \"FIRE\": \"#d85a30\"}\n}\n```\n\n| Field | Required | Meaning |\n|---|---|---|\n| `name` | yes | Display name. |\n| `description` | no | Free text. |\n| `dimensions` | yes | `1` (a row) or `2` (a grid). |\n| `states` | yes | The values a cell can take (see below). |\n| `neighbourhood` | yes | Which cells count as neighbours (see below). |\n| `edges` | yes | What lies beyond the grid: `{\"type\": \"wrap\"}` (opposite sides touch) or `{\"type\": \"fixed\", \"value\": <state>}`. |\n| `update` | no | How cells are updated. Only `\"synchronous\"` exists today: every cell is updated at once from the old grid. `\"movement\"` and `\"agents\"` are reserved for later. |\n| `parameters` | no | Named numbers that rules can use. An experiment can override them. |\n| `rules` | yes | Ordered list. For each cell, the **first rule that applies** decides its new value. |\n| `otherwise` | no | The value of cells no rule applies to. Default `\"self\"` (unchanged). |\n| `colors` | no | Colours for pictures (`\"#rrggbb\"`); ignored by the simulation. |\n\n### States\n| Form | Example | Notes |\n|---|---|---|\n| Named | `[\"OFF\", \"FIRING\", \"DYING\"]` | Names are words (letters, digits, `_`). Stored as 0, 1, 2… in file order. |\n| Integer | `{\"type\": \"integer\", \"min\": 0, \"max\": 3}` | `min` and `max` are optional. |\n| Real | `{\"type\": \"real\", \"min\": 0, \"decimals\": 2}` | `decimals` rounds every new value, which lets decimal grids settle exactly. |\n\n### Neighbourhoods\n| Value | Cells |\n|---|---|\n| `\"elementary\"` | 1D: left and right. |\n| `\"von_neumann\"` | 2D: the 4 cells above, left, right, below. |\n| `\"moore\"` | 2D: all 8 surrounding cells. |\n| `[[-1, 0], [0, 2], ...]` | Any list of offsets (row, column), or `[offset]` in 1D. |\n\n### Rules\n**When/then rule:** `{\"when\": \"<condition>\", \"then\": \"<new value>\"}`. Without `when`, the rule applies to every cell.\n\n**Table rule:** `{\"table\": {\"111\": 0, \"110\": 0, ...}}` lists patterns of *the neighbours plus the cell itself, in reading order* (for `\"elementary\"`: left, self, right) and the value each pattern gives. Patterns not listed fall through to the next rule. Write each cell as one character (`\"110\"`), or separate cells with spaces for named states (`\"ON OFF ON\"`). Tables need named states or integer states with both `min` and `max`.\n\n### The rule language\nRules are small expressions in Python syntax, evaluated for every cell at once.\n\n| Name | Meaning |\n|---|---|\n| `self` | The cell's current value. |\n| `left`, `right` | (1D) The neighbour on that side. |\n| `north`, `south`, `east`, `west`, `north_east`, `north_west`, `south_east`, `south_west` | (2D) One neighbour. |\n| `step` | The number of the generation being read (0, 1, 2, …). |\n| State names | e.g. `FIRE` (named states only). |\n| Parameter names | e.g. `p`. |\n| `nb` | Inside `count/sum/mean/min/max` only: each neighbour in turn. |\n\n| Function | Meaning |\n|---|---|\n| `count(x)` | How many neighbours make `x` true. `count(FIRE)` is short for `count(nb == FIRE)`. |\n| `sum(x)`, `mean(x)`, `min(x)`, `max(x)` | Of `x` over the neighbours, e.g. `sum(nb)`. |\n| `min(a, b, ...)`, `max(a, b, ...)` | With two or more arguments: cell by cell. |\n| `random()` | A number in [0, 1) from the run's seeded generator. |\n| `abs(x)`, `floor(x)`, `round(x)`, `round(x, digits)` | As usual. |\n\nOperators: `+ - * / // % **`, comparisons (chains like `2 <= count(A) <= 3` work), `and`, `or`, `not`, `x if c else y`, and bit operators `& | ^ ~ << >>`. State names are written without quotes. Whole-number states must stay whole: use `//` rather than `/`.\n\n### Examples\n```json\n\"rules\": [{\"then\": \"self - 4 * (self >= 4) + count(nb >= 4)\"}]\n```\nSandpile: a cell with 4 or more grains loses 4, and gains one per toppling neighbour.\n\n```json\n\"rules\": [{\"when\": \"count(nb == (self + 1) % 4) >= 2\", \"then\": \"(self + 1) % 4\"}]\n```\nCyclic automaton: move to the next value if at least two neighbours already hold it.\n\n```json\n\"rules\": [{\"then\": \"(rule >> (4 * left + 2 * self + right)) & 1\"}]\n```\nAny elementary rule, chosen by the parameter `rule`.\n\n---\n\n## Experiment file\n\n```json\n{\n  \"name\": \"Forest fire, grid from the brief\",\n  \"automaton\": \"../automata/forest_fire.json\",\n  \"size\": [4, 5],\n  \"initial\": {\"type\": \"text\", \"rows\": [\"TTTT.\", \"TT.TT\", \".TFTT\", \"TTTTT\"],\n              \"legend\": {\"T\": \"TREE\", \"F\": \"FIRE\", \".\": \"EMPTY\"}},\n  \"steps\": 8,\n  \"seed\": 42,\n  \"max_steps\": 1000,\n  \"store_generations\": true,\n  \"checkpoint_every\": 100,\n  \"parameters\": {},\n  \"questions\": [\n    {\"ask\": \"state_after\", \"n\": 2},\n    {\"ask\": \"stable\"},\n    {\"ask\": \"occurs\", \"rows\": [\"T....\", \".....\", \".....\", \".....\"]},\n    {\"ask\": \"count_after\", \"n\": 3, \"value\": \"TREE\"},\n    {\"ask\": \"cycle\"}\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n| Field | Required | Meaning |\n|---|---|---|\n| `name` | yes | Display name; also the name of the run folder. |\n| `automaton` | yes | Path to the automaton file, relative to this file. |\n| `size` | if not given by `initial` | `[cells]` in 1D, `[rows, columns]` in 2D. |\n| `initial` | yes | Generation 0 (see below). |\n| `steps` | yes | How many generations to simulate (and store). |\n| `seed` | no | Seed for random numbers. If missing, one is chosen and written into the run folder. |\n| `max_steps` | no | How far a run may go to answer questions (default 10,000). |\n| `store_generations` | no | Keep every generation on disk (default `true`). Needed for pictures. |\n| `checkpoint_every` | no | Save a checkpoint every N steps (default 100). |\n| `parameters` | no | New values for the automaton's parameters, e.g. `{\"rule\": 110}`. |\n| `questions` | no | The questions to answer (see below). |\n\n### The initial world\n| Type | Example |\n|---|---|\n| `text` | `{\"type\": \"text\", \"rows\": [\"..F..\", \".F.F.\"], \"legend\": {\".\": \"OFF\", \"F\": \"FIRING\"}}`. Rows without spaces: one character per cell; rows with spaces: one word per cell (`\"0 12 3\"`). Tokens not in the legend are read as states directly. |\n| `random` | `{\"type\": \"random\", \"weights\": {\"TREE\": 0.6, \"EMPTY\": 0.4}}`. Drawn from the seeded generator. Needs `size`. |\n| `single` | `{\"type\": \"single\", \"value\": 1, \"background\": 0, \"position\": [2, 3]}`. One cell set on a uniform background (default position: the centre). Needs `size`. |\n\n### Questions\n| `ask` | Extra fields | Answer |\n|---|---|---|\n| `state_after` | `n` | The grid after n steps. Works for any n once a deterministic run has entered a cycle. |\n| `count_after` | `n`, `value` | How many cells hold `value` after n steps. |\n| `stable` | – | The step from which nothing changes, or \"never\" (with the cycle that prevents it). |\n| `occurs` | `rows` (+ optional `legend`) | The first step showing this exact grid, or a certain \"never\". |\n| `cycle` | – | Where the repetition starts and how long the cycle is. |\n\nA question that `max_steps` was not enough to settle is answered \"Not decided\". For automata with random rules, answers about stability and cycles say that they are not guarantees.\n"
}
```

  "content": "# CelLab code guide\n\nThis guide explains what every file does, where the code for each part lives, and why it is built this way. The input file formats are in [FILE_FORMATS.md](FILE_FORMATS.md).\n\n## 1. The idea in one paragraph\n\nAn automaton is **data**, not code. An automaton file lists the states, the neighbourhood, the edges and the rules. The rules are small expressions such as `self == TREE and count(FIRE) >= 1`. One general engine reads any such file and computes the next generation for every cell at once with NumPy. Around the engine, a runner repeats the step, takes a **fingerprint** (hash) of every generation, saves **checkpoints** so a run can be stopped and resumed, and answers the **five questions** from the fingerprints. Randomness comes from **one seeded generator** per run, so the same seed always gives the same run.\n\n## 2. The layers\n\n```\n automata/*.json    experiments/*.json                         INPUT FILES\n        │                   │\n        ▼                   ▼\n ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n │ automaton.py   experiment.py                 │  1. LOADING: JSON → checked objects\n │ loading.py  states.py  grids.py              │     (all errors found here, before running)\n │ neighbourhood.py (resolve)                   │\n ├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n │ expressions.py   rules.py                    │  2. RULES: compiled rule objects\n ├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n │ engine.py   neighbourhood.py (views)         │  3. ONE STEP: old grid → new grid\n │ randomness.py                                │     (pure, apart from seeded random draws)\n ├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n │ runner.py   fingerprints.py   questions.py   │  4. A RUN: loop, fingerprints, answers\n │ storage.py                                   │     checkpoints, resume\n ├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n │ cli.py   render.py                           │  5. OUTSIDE: command line, pictures\n └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘\n        │\n        ▼\n runs/<experiment>/<date_time>/   automaton.json, experiment.json, checkpoint.npz,\n                                  fingerprints.bin, generations.bin, answers.json, status.json\n```\n\nEach layer only uses the layers above it. The engine never reads files, the loaders never touch NumPy grids of a run, and the command line contains no logic of its own.\n\n## 3. File by file (`src/cellab/`)\n\n| File | Job | Main names |\n|---|---|---|\n| `errors.py` | The error types. `InputFileError` carries the file and the field, so every message reads `file, field: problem`. | `CellabError`, `InputFileError`, `RuleError`, `StorageError` |\n| `loading.py` | Reads JSON files and turns pydantic's error lists into one readable message. | `read_json`, `validate`, `location` |\n| `states.py` | What a cell may hold: named states, integers or reals. Converts file values to numbers, formats them back, and checks every new grid. | `StateSpace`, `state_space_from_file` |\n| `grids.py` | Grids written as text rows (`\"TT.F\"` or `\"0 12 3\"`), with a legend. | `parse_grid`, `format_grid`, `split_row` |\n| `neighbourhood.py` | Neighbourhood offsets, direction names, and `GridViews`: the padded grid that hands out shifted copies. | `resolve_neighbourhood`, `GridViews` |\n| `expressions.py` | The rule language: checks expressions when files are loaded, evaluates them with NumPy during steps. | `compile_expression`, `Expression`, `EvalContext` |\n| `rules.py` | The two rule kinds. Both return \"applies here?\" and \"new value\" for every cell. | `ExpressionRule`, `TableRule`, `build_table_rule` |\n| `automaton.py` | Loads and checks an automaton file; compiles every rule. | `load_automaton`, `Automaton` |\n| `experiment.py` | Loads and checks an experiment file; builds generation 0 and the question objects. | `load_experiment`, `Experiment`, `make_initial_grid` |\n| `engine.py` | **One step**: old grid → new grid. The only simulation code. | `step` |\n| `randomness.py` | Seeds, the generator, saving and restoring its state. | `make_generator`, `generator_state`, `restore_generator` |\n| `fingerprints.py` | 16-byte hashes of grids, and the `History` that spots repeats and standstills. | `fingerprint`, `History` |\n| `questions.py` | The five questions: what each needs, when it's resolved, how it's answered. | `StateAfter`, `CountAfter`, `Stable`, `Occurs`, `Cycle` |\n| `storage.py` | Run folders: copies of the inputs, atomic checkpoints, append-only record files. | `RunFolder`, `RecordWriter` |\n| `runner.py` | The loop: start, step, fingerprint, store, checkpoint, stop on Ctrl+C, resume, answer. | `Run`, `RunState`, `RunResult` |\n| `render.py` | PNG, GIF and 1D space-time pictures of a run. | `render_run` |\n| `cli.py` | The `cellab` command: `check`, `run`, `resume`, `answers`, `show`, `render`. | `main` |\n\n## 4. How each part works\n\n### 4.1 Loading (automaton.py, experiment.py)\nLoading happens in three layers, each with its own kind of message:\n\n1. **JSON:** `read_json` reports the line and column of a syntax error.\n2. **Structure:** a pydantic model (`_AutomatonFile`, `_ExperimentFile`) checks required fields, unknown fields (typos like `neighborhood`), and basic types.\n3. **Meaning:** `build_automaton` / `load_experiment` check what pydantic can't:\n   - states are valid and not reserved words\n   - the edge value is a state\n   - parameters don't clash with state names\n   - every rule compiles, so an unknown name stops loading\n   - tables have the right pattern length\n   - the start grid and question grids fit the size, and so on\n\nThe result (`Automaton`, `Experiment`) contains no raw text any more. State names have become numbers, the neighbourhood is a tuple of offsets, and every rule is a compiled object.\n\n### 4.2 The rule language (expressions.py)\n- **Parsing:** Python's own parser reads the text (`ast.parse(..., mode=\"eval\")`). `_Checker` walks the tree and accepts only a whitelist: numbers, names, arithmetic, comparisons, `and/or/not`, `if/else`, and the known functions. Anything else (attributes, imports, lambdas, lists, strings) is rejected with a message. That makes the language **safe**: a file can never run arbitrary Python.\n- **Evaluation:** `_evaluate` walks the checked tree. Each name stands for a whole grid: `self` is the grid, `north` is the grid shifted by one row, `FIRE` is the number 2. So every operation works on all cells at once.\n- **Aggregates:** `count/sum/mean/min/max(x)` evaluate `x` once per neighbour, with `nb` bound to that neighbour's shifted grid, stack the results, and reduce over the stack.\n- **Random draws stay fixed:** `and`/`or` evaluate every part (no short-circuit), so the number and order of `random()` draws per step never depend on the data.\n- **Runtime errors** (division by zero, …) become `RuleError`s that name the rule: `rules[0].then ('1 // (self - self)'): divide by zero`.\n\n### 4.3 One step (engine.py)\n```\nvalues  = grid in a wide number type (no overflow surprises)\nviews   = GridViews(values, radius, edges)        # padded once\nwork    = value of `otherwise` for every cell     # usually \"unchanged\"\ndecided = all False\nfor each rule in file order:\n    applies, new = rule.evaluate(ctx)             # two full-size arrays\n    chosen = applies and not decided              # first matching rule wins\n    work[chosen] = new[chosen]                    # (checked: whole numbers etc.)\n    decided |= chosen\nreturn states.finish_step(work)                   # rounding, limits, final type\n```\n- Every rule is evaluated for every cell, then masked. That's fast with NumPy, and keeps random draws in a fixed order.\n- Everything reads the **old** grid, so cell order never matters: this is the synchronous update the brief describes.\n\n**Padding** (`neighbourhood.GridViews`): the grid is padded by `radius` cells, copied from the other side (`wrap`) or set to the edge value (`fixed`). A neighbour at offset `(dr, dc)` is the slice `padded[r+dr : r+dr+H, r+dc : r+dc+W]`, a view with no copying and no loop over cells.\n\n**Table rules** (`rules.TableRule`): each cell's pattern is turned into a number (reading the cells as digits in base *number of states*) and looked up in two arrays, `listed` and `results`, built when the file was loaded.\n\n### 4.4 Fingerprints and the five questions (fingerprints.py, questions.py)\n- `fingerprint(grid)` is a 16-byte BLAKE2b hash of the grid's shape, type and bytes. Two different grids collide with probability about 2⁻¹²⁸.\n- `History.record` keeps:\n  - `first_seen[fp] = first step`\n  - `repeat = (earlier, later)` the first time a fingerprint comes back\n  - `standstill`: the first step equal to the step before\n- **Key fact:** for deterministic rules, a repeat means the run is in a cycle forever, so it decides every question at once:\n\n| Question | How it is answered |\n|---|---|\n| `state_after(n)` | The kept grid of step n. Beyond the run, inside a cycle: the grid of step `start + (n − start) mod length`. |\n| `count_after(n, X)` | The same grid, then count X. |\n| `stable` | `standstill − 1`; or \"never\", if the cycle has length > 1. |\n| `cycle` | `repeat` gives the start and the length. |\n| `occurs(C)` | Look up C's fingerprint in `first_seen`. Once the cycle has closed without it: a certain \"never\". |\n\n- Each question also says which grids it needs kept (`capture_steps`) and whether the run has gathered enough (`resolved`). The runner keeps going until the experiment's `steps` are done and every question is resolved, or `max_steps` is reached. Unresolved questions are answered \"Not decided\".\n- **Random rules** have no such guarantee: the answers say so instead of claiming a cycle.\n\n### 4.5 Fixed randomness (randomness.py)\n- Each run has **one** `numpy.random.Generator(PCG64(seed))`. Nothing else in the code makes random numbers; a test checks the source code for it.\n- **Order of draws:** first the random initial world (if any), then every step one full-grid array per `random()` in the rules, in rule order.\n- **Missing seed:** if the experiment has none, `new_seed()` picks one and the run folder records it, so any run can be repeated.\n- **Saved state:** the generator's internal state is saved in every checkpoint, so a resumed run continues the same sequence.\n\n### 4.6 Saving and resuming (storage.py, runner.py)\n**A run folder** holds:\n- copies of both input files (with the real seed written in)\n- `checkpoint.npz`: step, grid, initial grid, seed, generator state, the kept grids, and the SHA-256 of `automaton.json`\n- two **append-only** files of fixed-size records: `fingerprints.bin` (16 bytes per step) and `generations.bin` (one grid per step). Generation k starts at byte `k × grid size`, so any step can be read directly.\n\n**Checkpoints are atomic:** written to `checkpoint.tmp`, then renamed over `checkpoint.npz`. A crash leaves either the old or the new checkpoint, never half of one.\n\n**Ctrl+C** only sets a flag (`runner._stop_requests`). The loop notices it between two steps, saves a checkpoint and stops cleanly. `--stop-at N` does the same at a chosen step.\n\n**Resume** (`Run.open`):\n1. Load the folder's own copies of the files.\n2. Refuse if `automaton.json` changed (its digest).\n3. Rebuild the `History` from `fingerprints.bin`.\n4. Cut both `.bin` files back to the checkpoint, dropping steps computed after a crash.\n5. Restore the generator, and continue with the same loop.\n\nThe tests check that the result is byte-for-byte the same as an uninterrupted run. They cover stops at several steps, Ctrl+C, and a simulated crash between checkpoints.\n\n**Trade-off:** each checkpoint forces the files to disk (`fsync`), which is slow on Windows. That's why the default is every 100 steps: at most 100 steps are recomputed after a crash.\n\n### 4.7 The command line (cli.py)\nEach command parses arguments and calls the library; there's no logic in `cli.py` itself. Library errors (`CellabError`) are printed as one line starting with `error:`, never as a traceback.\n\n## 5. Where to change things later\n\n| Future need | Where it goes | What does *not* change |\n|---|---|---|\n| A new automaton | A new JSON file | Any code |\n| A new function in rules (e.g. `sqrt`) | `expressions.py`: the checker (`check_call`) and `_call` | Everything else |\n| A new neighbourhood name | `NAMED_NEIGHBOURHOODS` in `neighbourhood.py` | Everything else |\n| Movement / agents (traffic with speeds, Langton's ant, predator–prey) | A new update mode: `engine.step` chooses the mode named in the file's `update` field (already validated, reserved values `movement` and `agents`) | Runner, fingerprints, questions, storage, CLI: they only see grids |\n| Deliverable 3 dataset | Loop over experiments with `parameters` overrides and `seed`s; read answers and `generations.bin` | Engine |\n| Deliverable 4 parser | Produce an automaton JSON file; `load_automaton` validates it | Everything else |\n| A graphical interface | Call `load_experiment`, `Run.start`, `run.advance(on_step=...)`, `render` | The library |\n| Changing the checkpoint contents | Raise `CHECKPOINT_FORMAT` in `storage.py` | Old runs are refused with a clear message |\n\n## 6. Tests (`tests/`)\n\nRun them with `python -m pytest`; all 193 run in about 15 seconds.\n\n| File | What it proves |\n|---|---|\n| `test_engine_reference.py` | The engine agrees with **independent, naive implementations** (`reference.py`: plain loops, no shared code) on random grids, for every example automaton and 7 elementary rules. |\n| `test_known_results.py` | Results known in advance: the brief's forest fire, sandpile and Rule 58 example; the Rule 30 cycle table and dataset rows from the Deliverable 1 slides; Rule 90 dying on 16 cells; traffic keeping its cars; the glider's 48-step cycle. |\n| `test_rule_language.py` | Every operator, function, direction and edge type on small grids; first-rule-wins; runtime errors (out-of-range values, fractions in whole-number states, division by zero). |\n| `test_validation.py` | Over 50 broken files are each rejected with the right field and message. |\n| `test_reproducibility.py` | Same seed gives the same run; different seeds differ; the seed is recorded; no other randomness exists in the code. Stopping (at several steps, by Ctrl+C, or a crash) and resuming equals an uninterrupted run, byte for byte. An edited automaton is refused. |\n| `test_questions.py` | Jump-ahead through a cycle (checked against 12,345 directly simulated steps), \"never\", \"not decided\", random rules, saved answers. |\n| `test_generality.py` | **No state name from any example appears in the code**; every example file loads and runs. |\n| `test_cli_and_storage.py` | Every command; run folder contents; generations on disk; replay without stored generations; pictures. |\n\n## 7. Glossary\n- **Generation / step:** generation 0 is the initial world; step k produces generation k.\n- **Synchronous update:** every cell's new value is computed from the old grid; the order of cells doesn't matter.\n- **Fingerprint:** a 16-byte hash identifying a grid.\n- **Cycle (start s, length L):** generation s + L equals generation s, and then everything repeats.\n- **Checkpoint:** a saved copy of everything that changes during a run.\n- **Run folder:** a self-contained record of one run, enough to replay, continue or draw it.\n"
}
```

# Images and SVG

This page explains more than just `<img src="photos/reef.jpg" alt="…">`. It covers how images move through the system, SVG rules, borders and shadows on images and how those export to PPTX, and what happens when you drop images in the editor. For information about fonts, see the `fonts.md` page.

## How images travel

Every image FILE goes into the artifact's asset store as an upload (Artifact `publish`, `file_path`, `asset:true`; or `upload_asset` where your tool lists that). The slide keeps only the reference that call returns (`/_blob/<id>`), written verbatim as the `src`. The one exception is a design system's picture copied into the deck with its install (`deck-files.md`, "A design system in the deck"): it is not uploaded, and its `src` is its path in the deck, `project/ds/<folder>/<path>`, with no leading `/`. The image data never goes through you and never into a slide: never write a `data:` URI, and never put base64 in a call or a reply. That keeps slide files small.

If you build a `deck.html` with the appifact-slides skill's `scripts/make.ts`, `src` is the file's path, relative to the `.html` file and under its folder or your working folder (each `--assets-from <dir>` adds a folder). The script checks each file, lists the ones to upload (it embeds svg and avif files itself), and takes each url back as `--asset <file>=<url>`. With no asset store, use its `--inline-images` flag, not the empty frames below. The comment at the top of the script lists the flags.

- `png`, `jpg`, `webp`, and `gif` files upload as they are. If a photo is much bigger than it will show on the slide, it is worth shrinking it first to about 2× its box.

- An `svg` file uploads too, and is shown with `<img>`. The store removes scripts, `<style>` blocks, animation, `<foreignObject>` and embedded images from an uploaded SVG. So style it with attributes, or export it as a PNG if it needs those. A small SVG (52 KB or less) can go into the slide as `<svg>` code instead (see SVG below).

- `avif`, `bmp`, and any other type the store refuses: convert the file to png or webp first, then upload that.

- If you can't upload, or the store still refuses a file, do not write the image into the slide yourself. Leave an empty frame where it belongs: `<img alt="what goes here" style="width:…; height:…">` with no `src`. It keeps its box, and the user can fill it in the editor (Add image…). Tell the user which images are missing.

Never use a URL in `src` — for example `src="https://…"`. Nothing fetches URLs. Save the image as a file and upload it.

Never Python’s eval.</p></div>\n</div>\n<div style=\"background:#16202B;border-radius:16px;padding:32px\">\n<p style=\"font-family:'IBM Plex Mono', 'Courier New', monospace;font-size:22px;line-height:1.45;color:#E3E8EC\">def check(self, node: ast.AST, inside_aggregate: bool) -&gt; None:<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;if isinstance(node, ast.Call):<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;self.check_call(node, inside_aggregate)<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;return<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;if not isinstance(node, _ALLOWED_NODES):<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;self.fail(f\"{type(node).__name__} is not allowed in rules\")<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;if isinstance(node, ast.Constant) and (isinstance(node.value, str) or not isinstance(node.value, (int, float))):<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;self.fail(\"only numbers and True/False can be written literally (write state names without quotes)\")<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;if isinstance(node, ast.Name):<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;self.check_name(node.id, inside_aggregate)<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;for child in ast.iter_child_nodes(node):<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;self.check(child, inside_aggregate)</p>\n</div>\n<p style=\"font-size:24px;line-height:1.4;color:#3F4A55\">Allowed: numbers, names, + − * / // % **, comparisons, and / or / not, if-else, and the functions count sum mean min max random abs floor round.</p>\n<aside>check is recursive: it checks a node, then all its children, so the whole tree is covered. check_call handles function calls separately: it only accepts our known functions, with the right number of arguments, and forbids an aggregate inside another aggregate. check_name rejects unknown names and suggests the closest known one, ignoring upper or lower case.</aside>\n</section>\n"
}
```

Two different grids collide with probability about <b>1 in 2¹²⁸</b>.</p>\n<p style=\"font-size:26px;line-height:1.45;color:#3F4A55\">Comparing 16 bytes is much cheaper than comparing whole grids, and storing them is cheap: a million steps take 16 MB.</p>\n</div>\n<div style=\"flex:1.15;display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:16px\">\n<div style=\"background:#16202B;border-radius:16px;padding:28px\">\n<p style=\"font-family:'IBM Plex Mono', 'Courier New', monospace;font-size:22px;line-height:1.45;color:#E3E8EC\">def record(self, fp: bytes) -&gt; None:<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;step = len(self.fingerprints)<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;if fp in self.first_seen:<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;if self.repeat is None:<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;self.repeat = (self.first_seen[fp], step)<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;else:<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;self.first_seen[fp] = step<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;if (self.standstill is None and self.fingerprints<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;and fp == self.fingerprints[-1]):<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;self.standstill = step<br>&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;self.fingerprints.append(fp)</p>\n</div>\n<p style=\"font-size:24px;line-height:1.45;color:#3F4A55\"><b>first_seen</b>: fingerprint → first step · <b>repeat</b>: first (earlier, later) pair · <b>standstill</b>: first step equal to the one before</p>\n</div>\n</div>\n<aside>History.record is called once per generation, step 0 included. Three small facts are all the five questions need: the first step each fingerprint appeared, the first time any fingerprint comes back (a repeat), and the first time a grid equals the grid just before it (a standstill). The if in record is wrapped over two lines here to fit the slide; in the file it is one line.</aside>\n</section>\n"
}
```

Not really. There's no supported way to hand a live Claude Code conversation to another person's account. Technically, he could copy the session file and try to resume it, but I wouldn't:

- **It's huge.** This conversation's file is about 13 MB. His Claude would start by squeezing it into a summary anyway, losing detail at random rather than keeping what matters.
- **It's tied to your machine.** Every tool result refers to `D:\CelLab` and Windows paths. On his Linux laptop those don't exist, so his Claude would keep tripping over them.
- **It isn't an official feature.** Copying session files between people is unsupported and could break at any update.
- **It's not needed for the logs.** The course only requires the conversations to be saved, and the hook already does that in `docs/ai-logs/`.

The reliable way to share context is a **`CLAUDE.md` file in the project root**. Claude Code reads it automatically at the start of every session in that folder, for you and for him. Combined with what's already in the repo, his Claude would start with the same picture yours has:

| File | What it gives his Claude |
|---|---|
| `CLAUDE.md` (new) | Project summary, current status, conventions (log everything, never push logs, plain slide titles, don't invent numbers, run the tests before committing), and pointers to the files below |
| `docs/GUIDE.md` | How the code works, file by file |
| `docs/FILE_FORMATS.md` | How to write automata and experiments |
| `docs/deliverables/D2-modeling/PLAN.md` | The Deliverable 2 plan and your Lab 5 notes |
| `explanation.md` (private, sent separately) | The fuller story, including Deliverable 1 decisions. It's out of date: it predates the engine. |

**One caveat:** a committed `CLAUDE.md` would be public in the repo. It holds working instructions, not your approach in detail, and the code itself becomes public once you push anyway. If you'd rather keep it private, the alternative is a git-ignored file you send him by hand, like `explanation.md`.

The professor's deck is finished, 14 slides: https://claude.ai/artifact/HCUmUTNMHHXBzx614HovcQ

I added the last four slides: the automata gallery, the Rule 30 freeze, how we checked correctness, and the live demo plan. Things I changed along the way:
- **Demo folder:** [demo/](demo/README.md) now holds the broken input files and the exact demo commands, with the expected output under each one. The demo no longer depends on the git-ignored `runs/` folder. I rehearsed every step and they all work.
- **Best demo moment:** the random Brian's Brain never settles; it repeats every 100 steps from step 750. Change `== 2` to `== 3` in its JSON file and it stops changing at step 6, with no code edited.
- **Wording fix:** cycle answers said "every 1 step(s)"; now they say "every step". All 195 tests pass. This and the demo folder are committed on `d2-engine` but not pushed.
- **Rule 30 slide:** I had written that with wrap-around edges it "never freezes". I checked: on 63 cells it doesn't repeat within 200,000 steps, so the slide now says exactly that.

## Do we need slides for D2?
Probably not required. Your Lab 5 notes say what to build, and only the final presentation mentions a ppt. I'd still bring the deck. It's about 8 minutes, then the live demo, and if the demo breaks, the slides show recordings of every command. If the professor only wants to see it run, jump to the last slide.

The link is private: share it from the page's Share menu, or download it as PDF/.pptx from the page.

## Password-protected files on GitHub
GitHub can't do this. Everything in a public repo is readable, and there are no per-file permissions. Options:
- **A second, private repo (recommended),** for example `cellab-notes`, with [member 2] added. Plans, logs and explanation.md go there, and the code stays public as the professor wants. At the end, give the professor access or hand in the logs as an archive.
- **git-crypt:** files are stored encrypted in the public repo and you share the key privately. It works, but file names stay visible, setup on Windows is fiddly, and losing the key means losing the files.
- **An encrypted 7-Zip archive** (AES-256 with `-mhe=on`, which also hides file names). Good for handing in logs once, impractical for daily work.

Anything already pushed is public, and the code itself shows our approach. A cheap way to protect it is what we're doing now: work on a local branch and push at each deadline.

## What could set us apart
Most teams will probably build a simulator with a few hard-coded automata, an LLM that turns text into rules, a neural network trained on something, and a GUI. To stand out, our extra work should use AI methods from the course rather than only an API call, come with measured numbers, and be memorable on presentation day.

**Our biggest unused advantage:** the engine computes the true answer to every question for any automaton. That makes three things cheap for us that are expensive for others:
- unlimited correctly labelled training data
- exact scoring of every AI component
- experiments on where AI works and where it doesn't

That points to a research question that links D3, D4 and the final: **when can a trained model replace simulation, and when can't it?** Rule 30 is in the brief as the hard automaton for a reason: it's believed that the only way to know its state far ahead is to run it. A small convolutional network (CNN) can represent one step of any of our rules exactly (Gilpin 2019), though training it to do that is harder than it sounds (Springer & Kenyon 2021). Predicting 50 steps ahead should work for simple rules and fail for Rule 30. A chart of accuracy against steps ahead, per automaton, is a real result. It also explains our design: AI to read and learn the rules, exact simulation to answer the questions.

**High value, low cost: do these**
1. **D3 dataset:** split the test set by automaton, not only by grid, so it tests whether the model handles rules it never saw. Add a one-page datasheet: how the data was generated, sizes, label balance.
2. **The CNN study above, with two baselines:** the exact engine, and an LLM asked the 5 questions directly without simulating. I expect the LLM to answer confidently and wrongly on Rule 30, and that one chart justifies the whole system.
3. **D4 parser with a repair loop:** the LLM writes the JSON, our checker returns its errors ("unknown name 'FIER' (did you mean 'FIRE'?)") and the LLM fixes them. Our error messages are already written well enough for this. Measure the success rate on the first try and after repairs.
4. **A parser test set for free:** generate English descriptions from our automaton files, parse them back, and compare behaviour (same fingerprints on random grids) instead of comparing text.
5. **The 5 remaining automata** (the agents mode), for 15/15. The professor said they'd do more.

**Medium cost, high impact**

6. **Ask only when it matters:** if a description is ambiguous (does "neighbours" mean 4 or 8?), run both readings. If the answers agree, answer; if they differ, ask one precise question. This is reasoning under uncertainty, and it's easy to demo.
7. **Rule induction:** show the system a few generations and it writes the automaton file. For elementary rules it reads off 8 table entries; for 2D Life-like rules it searches 2^18 candidates against what it observed. This could become a "guess the rule" game against the class.
8. **Inverse search with a SAT solver:** find a Game of Life grid that turns into "10" one step later. That's constraint satisfaction from the course, and a funny opening for the final. I haven't tried it yet. Some patterns have no predecessor at all ("Gardens of Eden"), which would make a good slide too.
9. **A GUI built around the questions:** a time slider over the stored states, the cycle drawn as a loop on the timeline, painting cells, and typing a description to watch it run.

**Extras**

10. **Romanian input,** with the professor describing an automaton live in Romanian.
11. **A short research write-up:** reproduce the Martin–Odlyzko–Wolfram (1984) cycle-length results for rules like Rule 90 on rings with our engine, plus the Rule 30 freeze and the CNN study.
12. **A one-page "how we used AI" reflection** drawn from the mandatory logs: where the AI was wrong and how we caught it.
13. **Continuous integration on GitHub:** the tests run on every push, with a status badge in the README.

Things I'd avoid:
- features without measurements
- depending on a paid API during the live demo (keep an offline fallback, given our laptops)
- spreading over too many extras

Items 1–5 cover D3 and D4 completely; for the final I'd pick two from 6–9.

## Installation

Python 3.11 or newer.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate          # Windows
source .venv/bin/activate       # Linux / macOS
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install -e .
```

`pip install -e .` makes the `cellab` command available (or use `python -m cellab`).

## Usage

```bash
cellab check automata/forest_fire.json experiments/forest_fire_brief.json   # validate files
cellab run experiments/forest_fire_brief.json                               # run + answer the questions
cellab run experiments/forest_fire_regrowth.json --seed 42 --trace          # print every step's fingerprint
cellab run experiments/rule30_ring16.json --stop-at 2000                    # stop early (or press Ctrl+C)
cellab resume runs/<experiment>/<date_time>                                 # continue where it stopped
cellab resume runs/<...> --steps 100                                        # run a finished run further
cellab answers runs/<...>                                                   # print the answers again
cellab show runs/<...> --step 3                                             # print one generation
cellab render runs/<...>                                                    # first.png, last.png, run.gif / spacetime.png
```

Each run gets a self-contained folder in `runs/` with copies of its input files (including the seed used), checkpoints, fingerprints, generations and answers.

## Documentation

- [docs/FILE_FORMATS.md](docs/FILE_FORMATS.md): how to write automaton and experiment files, including the rule language.
- [docs/GUIDE.md](docs/GUIDE.md): how the code is organised, how each part works, and where future changes go.

## 1. Citirea și verificarea fișierelor

| [errors.py](src/cellab/errors.py) | 36 | Tipurile de erori. `InputFileError` scrie mesajul ca „fișier, locație: problemă”. `RuleError` apare când o regulă produce o valoare nepermisă în timpul rulării. `StorageError` apare când folderul unei rulări e stricat sau nu se potrivește. |
| [loading.py](src/cellab/loading.py) | 68 | Citește JSON-ul și dă erori cu linia și coloana. Validează structura cu pydantic și transformă erorile lui în mesaje pe înțeles: câmpurile necunoscute primele, cu lista câmpurilor permise. |
| [states.py](src/cellab/states.py) | 163 | Ce valori poate lua o celulă, în trei variante: stări cu nume (EMPTY/TREE/FIRE), numere întregi cu limite (sandpile) sau numere reale cu zecimale (diffusion). Alege tipul numpy potrivit și citește/scrie valorile. După fiecare pas verifică rezultatul (rotunjire, limite) în `finish_step`. |
| [grids.py](src/cellab/grids.py) | 71 | Grile scrise ca text în experimente și în răspunsuri, de exemplu `"TTF"` sau `"TREE FIRE"`, cu o legendă pentru litere. |
| [neighbourhood.py](src/cellab/neighbourhood.py) | 92 | Ce vecini vede fiecare celulă: `elementary`, `von_neumann`, `moore` sau o listă proprie de poziții, plus numele direcțiilor (left/right, north/south…). `GridViews` bordează grila (wrap sau valoare fixă) și dă „vecinul de la poziția X” pentru toate celulele deodată, ca bucăți de array numpy, fără bucle. |
| [expressions.py](src/cellab/expressions.py) | 287 | **Cel mai lung modul: limbajul regulilor.** Un text ca `self == TREE and count(FIRE) >= 1` e parsat cu `ast`-ul din Python. `_Checker` permite doar operații din lista albă și sugerează corecturi („did you mean 'FIRE'?”). `_evaluate` calculează expresia pe toată grila cu numpy. Nu folosește niciodată `eval`, de aceea [fire_attack.json](demo/fire_attack.json) e respins. Conține și funcțiile `count/sum/mean/min/max` peste vecini, `random()`, `abs`, `floor`, `round`. |
| [rules.py](src/cellab/rules.py) | 107 | Cele două feluri de reguli: `ExpressionRule` (când/atunci) și `TableRule` (tabel model → rezultat, ca la Rule 30: `"111": 0`). Ambele răspund pentru fiecare celulă: se aplică regula aici și, dacă da, ce valoare nouă primește? |
| [automaton.py](src/cellab/automaton.py) | 203 | Citește fișierul automatului în trei straturi: JSON → structură → verificări de sens (stări, reguli, culori, parametri). Rezultatul e obiectul `Automaton`, gata de rulare. Calculează și un hash SHA-256 al fișierului și dacă automatul e determinist. Modurile `movement`/`agents`, pentru cele 5 automate rămase, sunt deja rezervate. |
| [experiment.py](src/cellab/experiment.py) | 281 | Fișierul experimentului: ce automat, cât de mare e grila, starea inițială (`text`, `random` cu ponderi sau `single`, adică o singură celulă), pașii, seed-ul, `max_steps`, cât de des se face checkpoint, parametrii suprascriși și întrebările. `make_initial_grid` construiește grila de start. |

## 2. Simularea

| Fișier | Linii | Ce rost are și ce conține |
|---|---|---|
| [engine.py](src/cellab/engine.py) | 65 | **Un pas: grila veche intră, grila nouă iese.** Totul se calculează din grila veche (actualizare sincronă), iar prima regulă care se potrivește câștigă; altfel se aplică `otherwise`. E scurt fiindcă greul e în modulele de mai sus. |
| [randomness.py](src/cellab/randomness.py) | 38 | Un singur generator aleator per rulare, creat din seed. Starea lui se salvează în checkpoint, așa că o rulare reluată continuă exact la fel. |
| [fingerprints.py](src/cellab/fingerprints.py) | 69 | Un hash de 16 octeți pentru fiecare grilă. `History` ține minte unde a apărut fiecare hash: un hash care se repetă înseamnă ciclu, iar un ciclu de lungime 1 înseamnă că grila e stabilă. |
| [questions.py](src/cellab/questions.py) | 242 | Cele 5 întrebări: `StateAfter`, `CountAfter`, `Stable`, `Cycle`, `Occurs`. Fiecare știe de ce pași are nevoie, când are un răspuns sigur și cum formulează răspunsul. Din ciclu sare direct la starea după 1.000.000 de pași, fără să-i simuleze pe toți. |
| [runner.py](src/cellab/runner.py) | 226 | Bucla care leagă totul. `Run.start` creează o rulare nouă. `Run.open` o reia: verifică hash-ul automatului și taie ce s-a scris după ultimul checkpoint. `advance` face pas, înregistrare, checkpoint și se oprește la Ctrl+C sau `--stop-at`. Continuă și după `steps` până răspunde la întrebări, cel mult până la `max_steps`. |
| [storage.py](src/cellab/storage.py) | 201 | Folderul unei rulări: copii ale fișierelor de intrare, `checkpoint.npz` (scris atomic, ca să nu se strice la crash), `fingerprints.bin`, `generations.bin`, `answers.json` și `status.json`. |

## 3. Interfața

| Fișier | Linii | Ce rost are și ce conține |
|---|---|---|
| [cli.py](src/cellab/cli.py) | 195 | Comenzile `check`, `run`, `resume`, `answers`, `show` și `render`. Doar apelează biblioteca, fără logică proprie. |
| [render.py](src/cellab/render.py) | 90 | Imagini pentru oameni: `first.png`, `last.png` și `run.gif` pentru automatele 2D, `spacetime.png` pentru cele 1D (fiecare rând e un pas). |
| [\_\_init\_\_.py](src/cellab/__init__.py) | 24 | Ce exportă pachetul, plus versiunea 0.2.0. |
| [\_\_main\_\_.py](src/cellab/__main__.py) | 5 | Permite rularea cu `python -m cellab`. |

Ordinea în care ți-aș recomanda să le citești: `engine.py` → `runner.py` → `questions.py` → `expressions.py`. Celelalte module sunt „unelte” pentru acestea patru.

## 5. Exemplele

**Automatele** (13): `forest_fire`, `forest_fire_regrowth`, `brians_brain`, `sandpile`, `cyclic`, `voter`, `crystal_growth`, `epidemic`, `diffusion`, `traffic`, `rule30`, `elementary` (oricare dintre cele 256 de reguli, alese printr-un parametru) și `game_of_life`.

**Experimentele** (19). Cele cu `_brief` folosesc grilele din enunț. Câteva cu rezultate pe care le-am verificat:

| Experiment | Ce arată |
|---|---|
| `forest_fire_brief` | Grila din enunț: stabilă de la pasul 5, 2 copaci după 3 pași |
| `sandpile_brief` | Se așază la 132 / 023 / 301, stabilă de la pasul 3 |
| `game_of_life_glider` | Un glider pe o grilă 12×12 cu margini legate: ciclu de 48 de pași |
| `rule30_ring16` | Ciclu de 6.016 pași care începe la pasul 58, plus starea după 1.000.000 de pași |
| `rule30_triangle` | Triunghiul clasic Rule 30; cu margini fixe se oprește complet de la pasul 175 |
| `brians_brain_random` | Nu se stabilizează niciodată: ciclu de 100 de pași de la pasul 750 |
| `traffic_brief` | Ciclu de 10 pași |

Celelalte: `brians_brain_brief`, `crystal_growth`, `cyclic_brief`, `cyclic_random`, `diffusion_brief`, `epidemic`, `forest_fire_regrowth`, `game_of_life_random`, `rule110_random`, `rule58_lab`, `sandpile_tower` și `voter_brief`.

## 6. Cum rulezi exemplele

Deschide PowerShell în `D:\CelLab`. Totul e deja instalat în `.venv`, deci doar activezi mediul:

```bash
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```

Dacă PowerShell refuză activarea, poți scrie peste tot `.venv\Scripts\cellab.exe` în loc de `cellab`.

Verifici un fișier:

```bash
cellab check automata/forest_fire.json experiments/forest_fire_brief.json
```

Rulezi un experiment și primești răspunsurile la întrebări:

```bash
cellab run experiments/forest_fire_brief.json
```

Același experiment, cu grila afișată după fiecare pas:

```bash
cellab run experiments/forest_fire_brief.json --show
```

La final, comanda scrie „Saved in runs\...\<data_ora>”. Copiază acea cale și folosește-o în locul lui `<cale>` în comenzile următoare.

Faci imaginile (`run.gif`, `first.png`, `last.png` sau `spacetime.png`), care apar în același folder:

```bash
cellab render <cale>
```

Oprești o rulare la pasul 120 și o reiei de unde a rămas:

```bash
cellab run experiments/forest_fire_regrowth.json --seed 5 --stop-at 120
```

```bash
cellab resume <cale>
```

Reafișezi răspunsurile sau o anumită generație:

```bash
cellab answers <cale>
```

```bash
cellab show <cale> --step 3
```

Rulezi toate cele 19 experimente deodată (durează cam un minut):

```bash
Get-ChildItem experiments\*.json | ForEach-Object { cellab run $_.FullName }
```

Rulezi testele:

```bash
python -m pytest
```

Pentru demo-ul de la D2, pașii exacți și ce trebuie să apară după fiecare comandă sunt în [demo/README.md](demo/README.md). Toate rulările se salvează în `runs/`, care nu ajunge pe GitHub, deci le poți șterge oricând.

Am rulat acum `sandpile_brief` ca să verific că totul merge și a dat exact rezultatul de mai sus.

```
"""Save the current Claude Code conversation into docs/ai-logs.

Run automatically by the Stop hook in .claude/settings.json after every
assistant reply. Reads the hook payload (JSON) from stdin, copies the raw
transcript (JSONL) and writes a human-readable Markdown version.

Can also be run by hand on any transcript:
    python tools/save_ai_log.py path/to/transcript.jsonl
"""
import json
import re
import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
RAW_DIR = ROOT / "docs" / "ai-logs" / "raw"
READABLE_DIR = ROOT / "docs" / "ai-logs" / "readable"
# App-injected context notes; kept in the raw copy, dropped from the readable one.
REMINDER = re.compile(r"", re.DOTALL)


def text_of(content):
    """Flatten a message's content (string or list of blocks) to Markdown."""
    if isinstance(content, str):
        return content
    parts = []
    for block in content or []:
        kind = block.get("type")
        if kind == "text":
            parts.append(block["text"])
        elif kind == "tool_use":
            args = json.dumps(block.get("input", {}), ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)
            parts.append(f"**[tool call: {block.get('name')}]**\n```json\n{args}\n```")
        elif kind == "tool_result":
            result = block.get("content")
            if isinstance(result, list):
                result = "\n".join(b.get("text", f"[{b.get('type')}]") for b in result)
            parts.append(f"**[tool result]**\n```\n{str(result)[:4000]}\n```")
        elif kind == "image":
            parts.append("*[image attached]*")
    return "\n\n".join(parts)


def to_markdown(transcript: Path) -> str:
    lines = [f"# AI conversation log: {transcript.stem}\n"]
    for raw in transcript.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
        try:
            entry = json.loads(raw)
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            continue
        if entry.get("type") not in ("user", "assistant") or entry.get("isMeta"):
            continue
        msg = entry.get("message", {})
        body = REMINDER.sub("", text_of(msg.get("content"))).strip()
        if not body:
            continue
        who = "User" if msg.get("role") == "user" else "Assistant"
        lines.append(f"## {who} ({entry.get('timestamp', '')})\n\n{body}\n")
    return "\n".join(lines)


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) > 1:
        transcript = Path(sys.argv[1])
    else:
        payload = json.load(sys.stdin)
        transcript = Path(payload["transcript_path"])
    if not transcript.exists():
        return
    RAW_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    READABLE_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    shutil.copyfile(transcript, RAW_DIR / transcript.name)
    (READABLE_DIR / f"{transcript.stem}.md").write_text(to_markdown(transcript), encoding="utf-8")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

}

# CelLab

AI course project: describe cellular automata in files, simulate them, and answer questions about their evolution.

Team: [member 1], [member 2].

## Installation

Python 3.11 or newer.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate          # Windows
source .venv/bin/activate       # Linux / macOS
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install -e .
```

`pip install -e .` makes the `cellab` command available (or use `python -m cellab`).

## Usage

```bash
cellab check automata/forest_fire.json experiments/forest_fire_brief.json   # validate files
cellab run experiments/forest_fire_brief.json                               # run + answer the questions
cellab run experiments/forest_fire_regrowth.json --seed 42 --trace          # print every step's fingerprint
cellab run experiments/rule30_ring16.json --stop-at 2000                    # stop early (or press Ctrl+C)
cellab resume runs/<experiment>/<date_time>                                 # continue where it stopped
cellab resume runs/<...> --steps 100                                        # run a finished run further
cellab answers runs/<...>                                                   # print the answers again

## The tests we have

There are two kinds: automated tests that run with one command, and checks I ran by hand.

### Automated tests: 195, all passing

| File | What it tests | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| [test_engine_reference.py](tests/test_engine_reference.py) | The engine against simple, slow versions written separately with plain loops, on random grids | all 2D automata, diffusion, all elementary rules, Rule 30 with fixed edges, traffic |
| [test_known_results.py](tests/test_known_results.py) | Answers we know in advance | forest fire and sandpile from the brief, Rule 58 from the lab, Rule 30 cycles from the D1 slides, the glider returning after 48 steps, traffic never losing cars, diffusion keeping total heat |
| [test_rule_language.py](tests/test_rule_language.py) | The rule language | edges (wrap and fixed), `count/sum/min/max`, first matching rule wins, division by zero reported, values outside the allowed states reported |
| [test_validation.py](tests/test_validation.py) | Over 50 broken files, each must be rejected with the right message | typos, missing fields, bad JSON (reports line and column), a missing file |
| [test_reproducibility.py](tests/test_reproducibility.py) | Seeds and resuming | same seed gives the same run; stop + resume, Ctrl+C, and a simulated crash all equal an uninterrupted run; resume refuses an edited automaton |
| [test_questions.py](tests/test_questions.py) | The 5 answers | state after 1,000,000 steps using the cycle, "not decided" when unknown, random rules never claiming a guaranteed cycle, singular/plural wording |
| [test_generality.py](tests/test_generality.py) | Nothing is automaton-specific | no state name (TREE, FIRE…) appears in the code; every example automaton loads and every experiment runs |
| [test_cli_and_storage.py](tests/test_cli_and_storage.py) | The commands and the run folder | `check`, `run`, `resume`, `show`, `--trace`, `render`; errors show a short message, not a Python crash |

## Running it yourself

Open PowerShell in the CelLab folder, either the app's Terminal panel or a normal PowerShell window after `cd D:\CelLab`.

### 1. Turn on the environment (once per terminal window)

```bash
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```

The prompt now starts with `(.venv)`. If PowerShell refuses, skip this step and write `.venv\Scripts\cellab.exe` instead of `cellab` and `.venv\Scripts\python.exe` instead of `python`.

### 2. Run the tests

Everything (about 12 seconds; ends with "195 passed"):

```bash
python -m pytest
```

Short output, only dots:

```bash
python -m pytest -q
```

Every test name with PASSED/FAILED:

```bash
python -m pytest -v
```

A single file:

```bash
python -m pytest tests/test_known_results.py -v
```

Only tests whose name contains a word:

```bash
python -m pytest -k glider -v
```

Stop at the first failure:

```bash
python -m pytest -x
```

Rerun only the tests that failed last time:

```bash
python -m pytest --lf
```

### 3. Check files
Checks automaton or experiment files without running them. "OK" means the file is valid; "ERR" names the file, where the problem is, and what's wrong:

```bash
cellab check automata/forest_fire.json experiments/forest_fire_brief.json
```

Try the broken examples to see the error messages:

```bash
cellab check demo/fire_typo.json demo/fire_spelling.json demo/fire_attack.json
```

### 4. Run an experiment
Runs it and prints the answers to its questions:

```bash
cellab run experiments/forest_fire_brief.json
```

Prints the grid after every step:

```bash
cellab run experiments/forest_fire_brief.json --show
```

Prints a fingerprint (hash) per step:

```bash
cellab run experiments/forest_fire_regrowth.json --seed 42 --trace
```

Overrides the experiment's seed or number of steps:

```bash
cellab run experiments/epidemic.json --seed 7 --steps 100
```

**Tip:** `--out` picks the run folder name yourself, so you don't have to copy the long dated path. The folder must not exist yet; delete it or pick another name.

```bash
cellab run experiments/forest_fire_regrowth.json --seed 5 --out runs/mine/fire
```

### 5. Work with a run folder
Prints the answers again:

```bash
cellab answers runs/mine/fire
```

Prints one saved generation (without `--step` it prints the last one):

```bash
cellab show runs/mine/fire --step 3
```

Makes pictures in the run folder: `first.png`, `last.png` and `run.gif` for 2D runs, `spacetime.png` for 1D runs.

```bash
cellab render runs/mine/fire
```

Opens the folder to look at them:

```bash
explorer runs\mine\fire
```

### 6. Stop and resume
Stops at step 120. Pressing Ctrl+C during any run does the same thing.

```bash
cellab run experiments/forest_fire_regrowth.json --seed 5 --out runs/mine/stopped --stop-at 120
```

Continues from where it stopped:

```bash
cellab resume runs/mine/stopped
```

Compares it with the uninterrupted run from step 4. Expect "no differences encountered". In PowerShell it must be `fc.exe`, because plain `fc` means something else there.

```bash
fc.exe /b runs\mine\fire\generations.bin runs\mine\stopped\generations.bin
```

Runs a finished run 100 steps further:

```bash
cellab resume runs/mine/fire --steps 100
```

### 7. Make your own experiment
Copy an existing one, edit it (size, steps, seed, questions), check it, then run it:

```bash
copy experiments\forest_fire_brief.json experiments\my_test.json
```

```bash
cellab check experiments/my_test.json
```

```bash
cellab run experiments/my_test.json --show
```

The format of these files is explained in [docs/FILE_FORMATS.md](docs/FILE_FORMATS.md).

### 8. Help and cleanup
Lists all commands, and the options of one command:

```bash
cellab --help
```

```bash
cellab run --help
```

Deletes all run folders. They are never pushed to GitHub, so this is always safe.

```bash
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force runs
```

The full demo for the professor, with the expected output after each command, is in [demo/README.md](demo/README.md).

## Assistant (2026-11-05T11:18:47.801Z)

## What the shifted views are for, using the forest fire

The forest rule says: **a tree catches fire if at least one of its 4 neighbours (north, south, east, west) is burning.** So for every cell the engine has to answer: how many of my 4 neighbours are FIRE?

### The slow way: a loop

For each cell, look north, south, east and west, and count the fires. On a 200×200 grid that is 40,000 cells × 4 lookups, one at a time in Python, which is slow.

### Our way: ask every cell at once

NumPy can compare whole grids in one operation, so instead of asking each cell "who is north of you?", the engine builds **a whole grid where every position already holds its north neighbour**. That's the "north view". It does the same for south, west and east, giving 4 views because the forest fire has 4 neighbours.

Think of it as 4 transparent copies of the grid, each slid one square in a different direction and laid over the original. Look down through any one square and you see the cell plus its 4 neighbours lined up on top of it.

### Worked example (the grid on the slide)

```
TTTT.
TT.TT
.TFTT      ← the fire F is at row 2, column 2
TTTTT
```

Take the tree at row 2, column 1 (just left of the fire). At that same position in each view:

| View | Contains | Value |
|---|---|---|
| north | the cell above it | T |
| south | the cell below it | T |
| west | the cell to its left | `.` (empty) |
| east | the cell to its right | **F** |

`count(FIRE)` = (north == F) + (south == F) + (west == F) + (east == F) = **1**. The cell is a tree and has at least 1 burning neighbour, so it becomes FIRE.

All of this happens for **all cells at the same time**. Each `view == FIRE` gives a grid of True/False values, and adding the 4 grids gives the fire count for every cell. Here 4 cells get a count of 1 (the 4 around the fire). 3 of them are trees, so 3 cells catch fire; that's the "3 cells decided → FIRE" in the slide's animation. The fire itself becomes EMPTY through the other rule.

### Why the padding

The cells on the border have no neighbour beyond the edge. The brief's forest says the outside counts as **EMPTY**, so the engine adds one ring of EMPTY around the grid first:

```
. . . . . . .
. T T T T . .
. T T . T T .
. . T F T T .
. T T T T T .
. . . . . . .
```

After that, every view is just a **slice of this padded grid** taken one square off-centre:
- north view = start one row higher
- south view = start one row lower
- west view = start one column to the left
- east view = start one column to the right

Each slice has exactly the original grid's size, and none of the data is copied. If the file says `"edges": "wrap"`, the ring is filled from the opposite side of the grid instead, so the grid behaves like a donut.

### Why this design is general

The engine doesn't know "4" or "forest". It builds **one view per neighbour listed in the automaton file**:

| Neighbourhood | Views |
|---|---|
| von Neumann (forest, crystal) | 4 |
| Moore (Brian's Brain, Game of Life) | 8 |
| elementary 1D (Rule 30) | 2: left and right |

The same code handles all of them, and a 200×200 step takes 1–3 ms.

In the code:
- **Padding and views:** `GridViews` in [neighbourhood.py](src/cellab/neighbourhood.py:78)
- **Counting:** `_aggregate` in [expressions.py](src/cellab/expressions.py:270)

**Separately:** the slide editor reports a problem on the demo slide (each numbered line has a `div` inside a list item), so you can't edit that slide's text in place. The slide still displays fine. I can rebuild it in a structure the editor accepts if you want to edit it yourself.

## User (2026-11-05T11:20:03.771Z)

does this work on every automaton or is this something we coded specifically for the tree example

## Assistant (2026-11-05T11:20:15.692Z)

It's general: nothing in it was written for the forest. The forest fire is only the example on the slide because it comes from the brief and is easy to follow by hand.

**How it adapts to each automaton:** the engine reads the neighbourhood and edge type from the automaton's JSON file, then builds one view per neighbour listed there.

| Automaton | Neighbourhood in its file | Views built | Edges |
|---|---|---|---|
| Forest fire, crystal growth, epidemic | `von_neumann` | 4 (N, S, E, W) | fixed EMPTY or wrap |
| Brian's Brain, Game of Life, cyclic, voter | `moore` | 8 (adds the diagonals) | wrap |
| Rule 30, Rule 110, Rule 58, traffic | `elementary` (1D) | 2 (left, right) | fixed 0 or wrap |
| Sandpile, diffusion | `von_neumann` | 4, with numbers in the cells instead of names | fixed |
| Any automaton | an explicit list of offsets in the file, e.g. `[[-2,0],[0,3]]` | one per offset; the padding gets wider for neighbours further away | fixed or wrap |

**What changes between automata is only what the rule does with the views:**
- Forest: `count(FIRE) >= 1` checks each view against FIRE and adds them up.
- Sandpile: `count(nb >= 4)` asks how many neighbours are toppling. The views are the same; the cells hold numbers instead of names.
- Diffusion: `mean(nb)` averages the 4 views.
- Rule 30: its table rule reads the left, self and right views to form a 3-cell pattern such as `110`, then looks up the result.

**How we know it isn't secretly forest-specific:**
- [test_generality.py](tests/test_generality.py) fails if any state name from any automaton file (TREE, FIRE, FIRING, CAR…) appears anywhere in the engine's code.
- [test_engine_reference.py](tests/test_engine_reference.py) compares this view method against a slow cell-by-cell loop for every example automaton, not just the forest.
- In the demo, changing Brian's Brain's rule in its file changes the behaviour without touching any code.

**Where it stops working:** the 5 automata we haven't done (Langton's ant, predator–prey, Schelling, falling sand, ecosystem). Their cells don't just read their neighbours and pick a new value: things move from one cell to another, and two agents can compete for the same spot. Shifted views can still be used to look around, but those automata need an extra update mode that moves things and settles conflicts. That's the planned "agents/movement" mode, and it's why they're listed as not done yet.

## Assistant (2026-11-05T11:22:02.424Z)

All 13 automata were built the same way: as one JSON file each in [automata/](automata/forest_fire.json), with no automaton-specific code. Each file lists the states, the neighbourhood, what happens at the edges, and the rules. The engine tries the rules in order and the first match decides; a cell that matches no rule stays as it is.

Below, "4 neighbours" means north/south/east/west (von Neumann) and "8 neighbours" adds the diagonals (Moore). "Wrap" means the grid's edges join up like a donut; "fixed" means everything beyond the edge counts as one value.

## From the brief

**1. Forest fire** ([forest_fire.json](automata/forest_fire.json))
- States: EMPTY, TREE, FIRE. 4 neighbours; outside the grid counts as EMPTY.
- Rules: FIRE → EMPTY. A TREE with at least 1 burning neighbour → FIRE.
- How: two rules, with `count(FIRE) >= 1` doing the neighbour check.

**2. Forest fire with regrowth and lightning** ([forest_fire_regrowth.json](automata/forest_fire_regrowth.json))
- Same states and neighbours, but wrap edges, with parameters `p = 0.02` (regrowth) and `f = 0.0002` (lightning).
- Rules: FIRE → EMPTY. A TREE catches fire if a neighbour burns, or with probability `f`. An EMPTY cell grows a tree with probability `p`.
- How: `random() < p` gives each cell its own random draw from the run's seeded generator, so the same seed gives the same run.

**3. Brian's Brain** ([brians_brain.json](automata/brians_brain.json))
- States: OFF, FIRING, DYING. 8 neighbours, wrap.
- Rules: FIRING → DYING → OFF. An OFF cell fires if exactly 2 neighbours are FIRING.
- How: three rules. This is the automaton whose `== 2` we change to `== 3` in the demo.

**4. Cyclic automaton** ([cyclic.json](automata/cyclic.json))
- States: the numbers 0–3 (parameter `levels = 4`). 8 neighbours, wrap.
- Rule: if at least `threshold = 2` neighbours hold the next value (`(self + 1) % levels`), the cell moves up to it, and 3 wraps back to 0.
- How: one rule using `nb` ("each neighbour") inside `count(...)`. From random cells it forms the spirals on the cover slide.

**5. Sandpile** ([sandpile.json](automata/sandpile.json))
- States: whole numbers of grains, 0 or more. 4 neighbours; outside the grid holds 0, so grains falling off the edge are lost.
- Rule: a cell with 4 or more grains topples, losing 4 and giving 1 to each neighbour. Every cell also gains 1 from each toppling neighbour.
- How: a single formula, `self - 4*(self >= 4) + count(nb >= 4)`, in which a True comparison counts as 1.

**6. Crystal growth** ([crystal_growth.json](automata/crystal_growth.json))
- States: EMPTY, CRYSTAL. 4 neighbours; outside the grid counts as EMPTY.
- Rule: an EMPTY cell with exactly `needed = 1` CRYSTAL neighbour becomes CRYSTAL. Crystals never disappear.
- How: one rule, with a parameter you can change in an experiment file. Started from one seed cell, it grows the snowflake pattern.

**7. Epidemic** ([epidemic.json](automata/epidemic.json))
- States: SUSCEPTIBLE, INFECTED_1, INFECTED_2, INFECTED_3, RECOVERED. 8 neighbours.
- Rules: a SUSCEPTIBLE cell with at least 2 infected neighbours becomes INFECTED_1. Then INFECTED_1 → INFECTED_2 → INFECTED_3 → RECOVERED.
- How: "infected for 3 steps" is modelled as 3 separate states, so no timer is needed.

**8. Voter model** ([voter.json](automata/voter.json))
- States: A, B. 8 neighbours, wrap.
- Rule: a cell takes whichever opinion most of its neighbours hold, and keeps its own on a tie.
- How: two rules comparing `count(A)` with `count(B)`.

**9. Diffusion / heat** ([diffusion.json](automata/diffusion.json))
- States: real numbers, 0 or more, rounded to 2 decimals. 4 neighbours, wrap.
- Rule: new value = (own value + the 4 neighbours) / 5, i.e. the cell averages with its neighbours.
- How: one formula using `sum(nb)`.

**10. Traffic** ([traffic.json](automata/traffic.json))
- States: EMPTY, CAR. 1D road using left and right neighbours, wrap (a ring road).
- Rules: a CAR moves right if the cell in front is EMPTY. An EMPTY cell receives the car from its left.
- How: two rules using the `left` and `right` directions. The movement is written as two cells each changing their own state, which is why it works without the agents mode. A test checks that cars are never created or lost.

**11. Rule 30** ([rule30.json](automata/rule30.json))
- States: 0 and 1. 1D, left/self/right, outside counts as 0.
- Rule: a table of the 8 possible patterns: 111→0, 110→0, 101→0, 100→1, 011→1, 010→1, 001→1, 000→0.
- How: a "table rule" instead of an expression. The brief's "hard" automaton.

## Extras

**12. Any elementary rule** ([elementary.json](automata/elementary.json))
- States: 0 and 1. 1D, wrap. Parameter `rule`, 110 by default.
- Rule: `(rule >> (4*left + 2*self + right)) & 1`. The 3 cells form a number from 0 to 7, which picks that bit of the rule number. This is exactly how the 256 rules are numbered.
- How: one file covers all 256 rules; an experiment just sets `"rule": 58` or `30`. We use it for Rule 58 from the lab and Rule 110, and D3's dataset can use it to generate examples for every rule.

**13. Game of Life** ([game_of_life.json](automata/game_of_life.json))
- States: DEAD, ALIVE. 8 neighbours, wrap.
- Rules: exactly 3 live neighbours → ALIVE. An ALIVE cell with exactly 2 live neighbours stays ALIVE. Everything else → DEAD.
- How: two rules plus `otherwise: DEAD`. It isn't in the brief; it shows that a new automaton is just a new file. The glider test checks that it returns to its start after 48 steps.

## The 5 not built yet
Langton's ant, predator–prey, Schelling segregation, falling sand and the artificial ecosystem. In each, things move between cells and can compete for the same spot, which needs the planned agents/movement update mode. The file format already reserves that mode.

## Assistant (2026-11-05T11:24:17.114Z)

Seeing the GIF for one automaton takes three commands: run it, render it, open it. Using `--out` gives the run a short folder name, so you don't have to copy the long dated path. Example with Brian's Brain:

```bash
cellab run experiments/brians_brain_random.json --out runs/mine/brain
```

```bash
cellab render runs/mine/brain
```

```bash
start runs\mine\brain\run.gif
```

The GIF opens in your default image viewer and plays. Run `.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1` first if the prompt doesn't start with `(.venv)`.

**For another automaton:** replace the experiment file and pick a new folder name, because the folder must not already exist. For example, the forest fire:

```bash
cellab run experiments/forest_fire_regrowth.json --out runs/mine/fire
```

```bash
cellab render runs/mine/fire
```

```bash
start runs\mine\fire\run.gif
```

**Running the same one again:** delete its folder first.

```bash
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force runs\mine\brain
```

**1D automata** (`rule30_triangle`, `rule58_lab`, `rule110_random`, `traffic_brief`) produce a still picture instead of a GIF, with one row per step:

```bash
start runs\mine\rule30\spacetime.png
```

**If you already ran the loop over all experiments,** the GIFs exist in `runs\all` and you can open them directly:

```bash
start runs\all\cyclic_random\run.gif
```

`rule30_ring16` is the only experiment with nothing to draw, because it doesn't save its generations.

## Assistant (2026-11-05T11:25:42.373Z)

It's one setting in the **experiment file**: `store_generations`. It defaults to `true`, and only one experiment turns it off, [rule30_ring16.json](experiments/rule30_ring16.json:9):

```json
"store_generations": false,
```

The setting is read in [experiment.py](src/cellab/experiment.py:46) and used in [runner.py](src/cellab/runner.py:170):

```python
writers = {"fingerprints": RecordWriter(...)}          # always saved: 16 bytes per step
if self.experiment.store_generations:
    writers["generations"] = RecordWriter(...)         # optional: the whole grid every step
```

So every run always saves its fingerprints, and only the full grids are optional.

## Why it's optional

**1. The questions only need the fingerprints.** Stable, cycle and "does it occur" are all answered by comparing hashes, and "state after N" uses the current grid or jumps through the cycle. The saved grids are only needed for pictures, `cellab show`, and looking back at old steps.

**2. Full grids get big fast; fingerprints don't.**

| Run | Fingerprints | All generations |
|---|---|---|
| Rule 30 ring, 16 cells × 6,074 steps | 97 KB | 97 KB |
| 200×200 grid × 10,000 steps | 160 KB | 400 MB |
| 1000×1000 grid × 10,000 steps | 160 KB | **10 GB** |

**3. D3 will need it.** To build the dataset we'll run thousands of experiments and keep only the answers. Saving every grid of every run would fill the disk for nothing.

**4. Nothing is lost.** Without saved grids, any old step can still be recomputed from the start, because runs with the same seed are always identical. That fallback is the `# Recompute from the start` branch in `grid_at`, [runner.py](src/cellab/runner.py:190).

## Why that particular experiment

Honestly, it isn't for space: 16 cells is tiny. It's there to **demonstrate and test the option**. It's the run that finds the 6,016-step cycle and answers "state after 1,000,000 steps" with fingerprints alone. It also wouldn't make a nice picture: a strip 16 cells wide and 6,074 rows tall.

## Seeing its picture anyway

There's no command-line switch for it yet, so make a copy of the experiment with the setting turned on:

```bash
(Get-Content experiments\rule30_ring16.json) -replace '"store_generations": false', '"store_generations": true' | Set-Content runs\ring16_stored.json
```

That copy is in `runs\`, but its `"automaton"` path is relative (`../automata/...`), and it still works from there because `runs\` and `experiments\` are both one level below the project folder.

```bash
cellab run runs\ring16_stored.json --out runs/mine/ring16
```

```bash
cellab render runs/mine/ring16 --until 150
```

```bash
start runs\mine\ring16\spacetime.png
```

`--until 150` draws only the first 150 steps, so the picture isn't 6,000 rows tall.

If you'd like, I can add a `--store` / `--no-store` option to `cellab run` so you don't need to edit files for this. It's a small change and a good fit for D3.

## Assistant (2026-11-05T11:29:25.033Z)

I added a bigger voter experiment, [voter_random.json](experiments/voter_random.json): a 120×120 grid starting with random A/B opinions, half each, for 40 steps with a fixed seed. I ran it and its animation is open in the Files pane.

**What happens:** the random noise clumps into large blue and orange regions within a few steps. The edges smooth out and the grid stops changing completely at step 31. At the end 6,980 of the 14,400 cells hold opinion A. Regions freeze instead of one opinion taking over because a cell only flips when most of its neighbours disagree.

**To run it yourself:**

```bash
cellab run experiments/voter_random.json --out runs/mine/voter_big
```

```bash
cellab render runs/mine/voter_big
```

```bash
start runs\mine\voter_big\run.gif
```

To run it again, first delete the folder:

```bash
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force runs\mine\voter_big
```

To try other variations, edit the file: a new `"seed"` gives a different random start, a bigger `"size"` such as `[200, 200]` gives a bigger grid, and different weights such as `{"A": 3, "B": 1}` give an uneven mix.

**A bug this turned up:** when I first edited the file with PowerShell, it saved the file with an invisible marker at the start (a "BOM"), and `cellab` refused to read it. Notepad and other Windows editors can add the same marker, so you could have hit this. The reader now accepts it, and I added a test for it. All 197 tests pass.

The new experiment and the fix are committed locally on `d2-engine` but not pushed. Say when you want them on GitHub.
